# Shepherd of Hermas — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Author** | Hermas (a Roman Christian freedman; possibly the brother of Bishop Pius I of Rome) |
| **Date** | c. 96–150 CE (composite; written over a long period) |
| **Audience** | The Roman Christian community |
| **Genre** | Apocalypse / moral allegory / pastoral manual |
| **Timeline** | Composed across the early-to-mid second century |
| **In One Sentence** | The longest and most popular early Christian text outside the New Testament — a vast, visionary tour through five visions, twelve moral mandates, and ten parables, built around one urgent pastoral question: is there forgiveness for Christians who have sinned after baptism? |

---

## The World Behind the Text

The Shepherd of Hermas is enormous. At 114 chapters (divided into five Visions, twelve Mandates, and ten Similitudes/Parables), it is longer than many books of the New Testament combined and dwarfs every other text in the Apostolic Fathers collection. It was almost certainly the most widely read Christian text of the second century outside the canonical Gospels and Paul's letters, and its popularity persisted for over 300 years. The fact that it is almost unknown to most modern Christians is one of the great ironies of canonical history.

The author identifies himself as Hermas, a freedman (former slave) living in Rome who received a series of visions. He has a family — a wife who talks too much, children who have apostatized — and a life of ordinary domestic complexity. He had apparently been involved in some kind of financial or moral failure in the past (the details are murky), and he is wrestling with the question of whether forgiveness is possible for such failures. This is not abstract theology — it is autobiography pressing itself into apocalyptic form.

The world of the text is the Roman Christian community of the second century: a community large enough to have structure and officers (the elders and deacons are mentioned frequently), diverse enough to contain wealthy members and poor ones, and troubled enough to need sustained moral exhortation. The community knows persecution — the figure of the great beast in the fourth Vision is understood as representing Rome's power — but the more immediate threat is internal: worldliness, wealth-love, double-mindedness (Greek: dipsychia, literally "double-souled"), and the moral complacency of those who assume their initial conversion guarantees salvation regardless of subsequent behavior.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

The pastoral question driving the entire text is explicit: what happens to people who sin after baptism? Early Christian theology had inherited a stark framework: baptism washed away all prior sins, but post-baptismal sin was a serious problem. Some argued there was no second forgiveness; others were more hopeful but uncertain. Hermas receives his answer in Mandate 4, from the figure of the Shepherd (the "angel of repentance"), and it is carefully calibrated: there is one more opportunity for repentance after baptism, but only one, and it will not be available indefinitely. The window of second repentance is open now, while the Shepherd is alive to proclaim it, but it will close.

This teaching was both liberating and urgent. It was liberating because it said: yes, you can come back, no matter how badly you have fallen. It was urgent because it said: do not delay. The combination of mercy and urgency is the pastoral genius of the book, and it explains its enormous popularity in communities that were watching members lapse, apostatize under pressure, or simply drift into moral indifference.

The book also serves as a sustained program of moral formation. The twelve Mandates are essentially a catechism of Christian virtues and vices — faith, temperance, truthfulness, patience, chastity, the avoidance of double-mindedness and grief, the testing of true and false prophecy, fear of God, and proper prayer. The Similitudes extend this through a series of elaborate parables that are as complex and layered as anything in the canonical Gospels. Together, the Mandates and Similitudes constitute a comprehensive guide to the Christian moral life.

---

## How to Read This Book

The Shepherd of Hermas rewards reading in stages rather than all at once. It is long, repetitive, and somewhat loosely constructed — it reads like a text that accumulated over time, with earlier visions revised and later material added. Do not expect the tight logical structure of a Pauline letter or the narrative momentum of a gospel.

Begin with the five Visions (chapters 1–25). The first four center on an aged woman who appears to Hermas in a series of revelations. In Vision 1 she is very old and frail; in Vision 2 she is older but sitting; in Vision 3 she is younger and more joyful; in Vision 4 she is young and beautiful. This transformation represents the progressive renovation of the church through repentance. The woman, Hermas comes to understand, is the Church herself — pre-existent and feminine (connecting here to 2 Clement's theology of the pre-existent female Church). Vision 5 introduces the Shepherd himself, the "angel of repentance," who will be Hermas's guide for the rest of the book.

The most important single episode is Vision 3's central image: the Tower. Hermas sees an enormous tower being built over water with shining square stones. The tower is the Church; the stones are different categories of Christians; the water is baptism. Some stones fit perfectly (faithful Christians who have stood firm); others are rejected and laid aside (those who have fallen away or are living worldly lives). The elaborate taxonomy of stones becomes a way of sorting the entire moral landscape of the Roman Christian community.

Read the Similitudes (parables) with patience — especially Similitude 9, which is the longest parable in early Christian literature and revisits the Tower vision with extraordinary elaboration. The mountain with twelve peoples, the twelve virgins representing virtues, the twelve women as vices — it is a complex moral typology that deserves careful mapping.

Read Mandate 11 on prophecy carefully: the criteria for distinguishing true from false prophecy are remarkably sociological — the true prophet does not speak only when asked by individuals (that is the mark of a mantis, a pagan diviner), does not charge money, does not speak in private consultations, but speaks publicly in the assembly, moved by the angel of God. This is a sophisticated, practically useful set of tests.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

The Tower-as-Church vision connects Hermas to 1 Corinthians 3:10–15 (Paul's image of building on the one foundation), to 1 Peter 2:4–5 ("living stones"), and to Ephesians 2:20–22. But Hermas develops the image more elaborately than any New Testament text, and his taxonomy of different kinds of stones becomes one of the most systematic early Christian treatments of the diversity of moral states within the community.

The two-angel theology of Mandate 6 — the angel of righteousness and the angel of wickedness, who wage war for influence over each human heart — connects to the Jewish tradition of the yetzer hatov (good inclination) and yetzer hara (evil inclination) in rabbinic theology, to the Two Ways tradition in the Didache and Barnabas, and to later developed angelology in both Christian and Jewish mysticism.

The concept of dipsychia ("double-mindedness" or "double-souledness") is one of Hermas's most distinctive contributions to Christian moral vocabulary. It appears nowhere in the New Testament with this precise technical sense, though James 1:8 ("a double-minded man is unstable in all his ways") is closely related. For Hermas, dipsychia is the root of almost all spiritual failures — the state of a person who half-believes and half-doubts, who prays without faith, who has one foot in the church and one foot in the world.

The Shepherd himself — the figure who guides Hermas — may be an influence on later Christian artistic and literary tradition. The image of the Good Shepherd carrying a sheep on his shoulders is one of the most common motifs in early Christian catacombs art, and while the Gospel tradition (Luke 15, John 10) provides the primary source, the Shepherd of Hermas may have reinforced and popularized this image.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

The most important thing to understand about the Shepherd is its status in the second and third centuries. This was not a fringe text. Irenaeus of Lyon cited it as "scripture." Clement of Alexandria quoted it frequently. Origen regarded it as highly useful, if not canonical. Tertullian, who initially accepted it, later rejected it furiously (as a Montanist, he regarded its permissive approach to post-baptismal repentance as dangerously lax). Athanasius recommended it for catechetical use. It appears in Codex Sinaiticus after the New Testament. For 300 years, this book was read in Christian communities as a text of near-scriptural authority.

Modern readers will find the text's repetitiveness frustrating, but this repetition is itself significant — it reflects the oral culture of transmission in which these texts lived. The same moral points are made multiple times in different forms, from different angles, because the author knows that moral formation happens through repeated encounter, not single exposure.

The angelology is dense and needs unpacking. There are multiple categories of angels: the six angels of creation who oversee the tower's construction, the seven archangels, the angel of repentance (the Shepherd), guardian angels of nations and of individual believers. This elaborate angelic hierarchy connects Hermas to Jewish apocalyptic (1 Enoch, Daniel) and to the broader Hellenistic interest in intermediary beings. It is not aberrant mysticism — it is mainstream second-century theological cosmology.

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

The Shepherd was included in Codex Sinaiticus (along with Barnabas), which confirms it was canonical or near-canonical in at least one important fourth-century community. Eusebius listed it among disputed books, noting both its wide use and the doubt about its apostolic origin — Hermas was clearly not an apostle, and the Muratorian Fragment (possibly late second century) explicitly argues it should not be read publicly in church because it was written "recently."

The timing argument proved decisive. The canonical process required apostolic origin (real or plausible), and Hermas had none. The Muratorian Fragment's concern — that it was written "recently" — reflects a growing consensus that the apostolic era was closed and that texts written after it, however valuable, were not scripture. By the time Athanasius made his definitive list in 367 CE, the Shepherd was firmly outside the canon, though still recommended for instructional use.

The Ethiopian Orthodox canon's broader scope does not include the Shepherd specifically, though various Eastern canon lists give it different statuses. Today it is universally recognized as the most important and revealing document of second-century Roman Christianity, essential for understanding the pastoral, theological, and social life of the early church.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| c. 96–100 CE | Earliest possible date for first Visions (Hermas may have known Clement of Rome) |
| c. 100–150 CE | Text grows through multiple stages of composition |
| c. 140–154 CE | Hermas possibly brother of Bishop Pius I (per Muratorian Fragment) |
| c. 150–200 CE | Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen all treat text as authoritative |
| c. 200 CE | Muratorian Fragment objects to its reading in public worship |
| c. 207 CE | Tertullian rejects it after joining Montanism |
| c. 350 CE | Included in Codex Sinaiticus after the New Testament |
| c. 367 CE | Athanasius excludes it from canon; recommends for instruction |
| c. 400–600 CE | Gradually falls out of regular use in the West |
| 1859 CE | Codex Sinaiticus rediscovered; Shepherd's full text recoverable |

---

*— HESED, Reader's Guide Division*
